- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥ 0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤ 0.33) and price is rising, model often fails to recognize reversal; adjust downward early in the forecast horizon.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >70% from prior peak), model frequently overshoots and fails to correct; apply a “cool-down” buffer or reduce forecast growth rate.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model often drifts toward mean reversion; anchor forecast near recent 5–7 day average if no strong sentiment bias.
- If true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 day pullback after peak), model tends to ignore it; add a “reversion penalty” or reduce forecast slope after peak.
- Model often underestimates volatility in bearish sentiment periods; increase forecast variance or add downward bias if sentiment is consistently low.
- Forecast horizon 30d is prone to lagging sentiment shifts; if sentiment turns bearish mid-horizon, adjust forecast downward by 1–2 days early.
- If sentiment history shows repeated “bullish → bearish” transitions, model tends to overreact; apply smoothing or dampen forecast changes during sentiment shifts.
